title: From early experiments to BrainGate
text:
CHAPTER 14  BRAIN-COMPUTER INTERFACES

14_01  FROM EARLY EXPERIMENTS TO BRAINGATE

A brain-computer interface (BCI), also called a brain-machine interface, is a system that measures brain activity and converts it into commands for an external device, bypassing the normal output pathways of nerves and muscles. For a mechatronics student it is a familiar architecture: a sensor (electrodes), signal conditioning (amplifiers, filters, spike detection), a decoder (an estimator or classifier), and an actuator (a cursor, robotic arm, speech synthesiser, or the user's own muscles stimulated electrically), all closed in a loop through the user's perception of the result. What makes BCIs unique is that the controller at the other end of the loop is a human brain that learns, adapts and gets tired. This section traces the field from its first experiments to the BrainGate clinical trials; the next two cover decoding algorithms and the current industry.

It is worth noting first that the most widely used neural interface is not a cortical BCI but the cochlear implant, which stimulates the auditory nerve with electrode arrays inserted in the cochlea to give hearing to people with profound deafness. Hundreds of thousands of people have received one. It is an input device rather than an output device, and it shows that the brain can learn to use crude, artificial signals, a lesson that runs through this chapter.

OPERANT CONDITIONING OF NEURONS

The first demonstration that a primate could learn to control a single neuron for reward came from Eberhard Fetz, who reported in Science in 1969 that monkeys rewarded when a cortical neuron's firing rate increased, and given feedback via a meter or clicks, learned to drive that neuron's activity up. This was biofeedback at the level of single cells. Its implication was profound: the decoder need not perfectly understand what a neuron normally does, because the brain can learn to change neural activity to achieve a goal. That theme of co-adaptation between brain and decoder returns repeatedly.

The phrase "brain-computer interface" was used by Jacques Vidal of the University of California, Los Angeles, in a 1973 paper in the Annual Review of Biophysics and Bioengineering titled "Toward direct brain-computer communication", which discussed using EEG signals, including evoked potentials, to communicate with a computer.

NON-INVASIVE BCIs FROM EEG

Because EEG (Chapter 10) needs no surgery, much early BCI work used it. Three signal families dominate:

Event-related potentials. Lawrence Farwell and Emanuel Donchin described in 1988 a speller based on the P300, a positive deflection about 300 ms after a rare, attended stimulus. Letters are arranged in a grid, rows and columns flash in random order, and when the row or column containing the user's intended letter flashes, the P300 is larger. Averaging over repeated flashes and classifying the responses identifies the letter. Speeds are modest, a few characters per minute in many studies, but reliability can be good.

Sensorimotor rhythms. Imagining or attempting a movement suppresses the mu (about 8 to 12 Hz) and beta rhythms over the corresponding motor cortex, called event-related desynchronisation. Jonathan Wolpaw, Dennis McFarland and colleagues at the Wadsworth Center trained people from the early 1990s to control a cursor in one and then two dimensions by modulating these rhythms. Gert Pfurtscheller's group in Graz developed similar systems based on motor imagery.

Steady-state visually evoked potentials. Looking at a light flickering at a given frequency produces EEG power at that frequency over visual cortex. Several targets flickering at different frequencies can be distinguished, giving relatively fast selection.

Niels Birbaumer and colleagues reported in Nature in 1999 that two people with advanced amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) learned, over months of training, to control slow cortical potentials enough to select letters with a "thought translation device", communicating messages. This was a powerful demonstration for people with no other means of communication, though the speed was very slow.

The fundamental limit of EEG is information: the skull and scalp blur and attenuate signals, so EEG reflects the summed activity of large populations (Chapter 10), and signals are contaminated by muscle and eye artefacts. Communication rates are therefore limited compared with intracortical recording.

INVASIVE RECORDING IN ANIMALS

The leap in performance came from recording many single neurons at once with implanted electrodes (Chapter 10), combined with the population coding ideas of 13_01.

In 1999 John Chapin, Miguel Nicolelis and colleagues reported in Nature Neuroscience that rats could control a robotic lever arm to obtain water using signals from populations of neurons in motor cortex and thalamus, and that some rats continued to do so while their own forelimb movements diminished.

In 2000 Johan Wessberg, Nicolelis and colleagues reported in Nature that the hand trajectories of owl monkeys could be predicted in real time from ensembles of cortical neurons using linear models and artificial neural networks, and used to move a robotic arm, including one at a remote location over the internet.

In 2002 two papers showed closed-loop control of cursors by monkeys. Mijail Serruya, John Donoghue and colleagues reported in Nature that a monkey could move a computer cursor to targets using a linear decoder applied to a small number of motor cortex neurons recorded with a multielectrode array, with performance close to that achieved by hand. Dawn Taylor, Stephen Helms Tillery and Andrew Schwartz reported in Science that monkeys controlled a cursor in three dimensions with a population vector decoder, and that performance improved as the decoder and the brain adapted to each other.

In 2003 Jose Carmena, Nicolelis and colleagues reported in PLoS Biology that monkeys learned to reach and grasp with a robotic arm controlled by neural ensembles, and that neuronal tuning properties changed as the animals learned, again showing brain plasticity in the loop.

In 2008 Meel Velliste, Schwartz and colleagues reported in Nature that monkeys could control a robotic arm with a gripper to feed themselves pieces of food, using a population vector decoder. Video of the experiment became one of the iconic images of the field.

The workhorse sensor in much of this work, and in human trials, has been the Utah array, a 4 by 4 millimetre grid of 100 silicon microelectrodes, about 1 to 1.5 millimetres long, developed by Richard Normann and colleagues at the University of Utah. It is inserted pneumatically into cortex and records spikes and local field potentials from the tips.

EARLY HUMAN IMPLANTS

Philip Kennedy and Roy Bakay developed a "neurotrophic electrode", a glass cone containing wires into which neurites grow, and reported in 1998 that a patient with locked-in syndrome could use signals from it to control a cursor. These were small, pioneering studies with few channels.

BRAINGATE

The BrainGate pilot clinical trial, initially organised around a company, Cyberkinetics, founded by Donoghue and colleagues, and later continued by an academic consortium including Brown University, Massachusetts General Hospital, Stanford, Case Western Reserve University and the Providence VA, implanted Utah arrays in the motor cortex of people with tetraplegia from spinal cord injury, brainstem stroke or ALS.

In 2006 Leigh Hochberg, Donoghue and colleagues reported in Nature that the first participant, Matthew Nagle, who had a cervical spinal cord injury, could control a computer cursor, open simulated email, operate a television and open and close a prosthetic hand using neuronal ensemble activity recorded from motor cortex, years after his injury. A key finding was that motor cortex neurons were still modulated by intended movements long after paralysis, so the signal source survives.

In 2012 Hochberg and colleagues reported in Nature that two participants with tetraplegia from brainstem stroke could reach and grasp with robotic arms in three dimensions. One participant, about 15 years after her stroke, used a robotic arm to pick up a bottle and drink coffee from it, the first time she had done so on her own since the stroke.

In the same period, Andrew Schwartz's team at the University of Pittsburgh reported in The Lancet in 2013 (Jennifer Collinger and colleagues) that a woman with tetraplegia controlled a robotic arm with seven degrees of freedom using two Utah arrays, and later work added more dimensions of hand control. In 2016 Sharlene Flesher, Robert Gaunt and colleagues reported in Science Translational Medicine that intracortical microstimulation of somatosensory cortex in the same group's participant produced sensations perceived as coming from his own paralysed hand, a step toward bidirectional BCIs that provide touch feedback.

Instead of a robotic arm, a BCI can drive the person's own muscles. Chad Bouton and colleagues at Battelle and Ohio State reported in Nature in 2016 that a man with cervical spinal cord injury could control hand and wrist movements via a sleeve of electrodes stimulating his forearm muscles, driven by decoded motor cortex activity. In 2017 A. Bolu Ajiboye, Robert Kirsch and colleagues in the BrainGate consortium reported in The Lancet that a participant controlled reaching and grasping of his own arm through implanted functional electrical stimulation.

Typing speed became a key benchmark. Chethan Pandarinath, Paul Nuyujukian, Jaimie Henderson, Krishna Shenoy and colleagues reported in eLife in 2017 point-and-click typing by BrainGate participants at rates around 8 words per minute in one case, a large improvement over earlier systems. In 2021 Francis Willett, Shenoy, Henderson and colleagues reported in Nature that a participant could write at about 90 characters per minute by attempting to handwrite letters, with the neural activity decoded by a recurrent neural network, roughly comparable to typing speeds on a smartphone for people of his age group. That work leads naturally into the decoding methods of 14_02 and the speech neuroprostheses of 14_03.

PRACTICAL PROBLEMS

Several problems kept BCIs in the laboratory for decades:

Signal stability. Neurons recorded on a given electrode can change from day to day as the array micro-moves, and the tissue response to implanted electrodes, including glial scarring, can degrade recordings over months to years, though some Utah arrays have recorded useful signals for many years.

Recalibration. Decoders often needed retraining each session, consuming the user's time.

Hardware. Early systems used a percutaneous connector, a pedestal through the skull and scalp, with cables to racks of computers. This was a risk of infection and impractical for home use. Wireless, fully implanted systems were a key engineering goal.

Speed and accuracy. Communication rates long lagged behind able-bodied typing or speech.

Many of these were the focus of the next generation of academic and commercial efforts.

CONNECTIONS TO AI AND MACHINE LEARNING

1. The decoder is a learned model. From linear regression in 2000 to recurrent networks in 2021, BCI history parallels machine learning history. Better learning algorithms translated directly into faster communication for paralysed people.

2. Two learners in the loop. Fetz's monkeys, Taylor's co-adaptive decoder and Carmena's changing tuning curves show that a BCI is a system with two adaptive agents: the brain and the algorithm. This is a multi-agent learning problem, and it raises questions also found in human-AI interaction: should the algorithm adapt to the user, or the user to the algorithm, and how fast, so that neither chases the other unstably?

3. Reinforcement learning and the brain as optimiser. The user learns from feedback (did the cursor hit the target?), exactly a reinforcement learning setup, with the reward prediction error machinery of Chapter 6 presumably at work. Some researchers have explored decoders that themselves learn from reinforcement signals, including error-related potentials detected in the brain when the user sees a mistake.

4. Distribution shift. Neural signal drift between days is a form of non-stationarity, the same problem as dataset shift in deployed ML. Methods from domain adaptation and from aligning latent dynamics across days (14_02) are used to cope.

5. Representations survive. That motor cortex remains tuned to intended movements years after paralysis means the learned "model" in the brain is preserved even when its output is disconnected, a striking parallel to how a trained network's internal representations persist even if its output head is removed and replaced.

SUMMARY

BCIs grew from Fetz's operant conditioning of single neurons in 1969, through EEG spellers and cursor control, to multielectrode decoding in rats and monkeys around 2000, and to the BrainGate and Pittsburgh human trials, in which people with paralysis controlled cursors, robotic arms and their own muscles. The central lessons are that intended movement signals persist after paralysis, that brain and decoder co-adapt, and that decoder quality, a machine learning problem, sets performance.
